```{r}
library(tidyverse)

```


### My Procedure

For my analysis, i will use median income after taxes,
because we want to measure the impact of energy prices on people's 
disposable income. 


### Income data per price region

To identify how the price hikes affected the different price regions, 
we will combine median households for counties in the same price areas.

```{r}

median_incomes <- read_delim("Inntekt_fylke_median_etter_skatt.csv",
    skip = 1,
    locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"),
    delim = ";",
    na = ".")


median_incomes <- median_incomes |>
    select(-"type of household") |>
    pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("Income"),
        names_to = "year",
        values_to = "median_income",
        names_prefix = "Income after taxes, median \\(NOK\\) ")

median_incomes <- median_incomes |>
    mutate(
        region = word(str_remove(region, "^[0-9]+\\s+"), 1)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(median_income))


```

As we can see, there are gaps in data for several counties.
This was due to a policy of merging together counties, 
three of which were seperated again. 

In these cases, I will act like merged counties were always there, by creating a "mock median" using weighted averages of medians from the previous counties, where each weight
reflects a previous county's population share. 

Price zones haven't changed during the scope of this analysis. 

Extracting population data for each county. 
```{r}
county_pops <- read_delim("Befolkning_etter_fylke.csv",
        skip = 1,
        locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"),
        delim = ";",
        na = "0")


county_pops <- county_pops |>
    pivot_longer(cols = contains("Befolkning"),
        names_to = "year",
        values_to = "population",
        names_pattern = "^([0-9]+)")

county_pops <- county_pops |>
    mutate(
        region = word(str_remove(region, "^[0-9]+\\s+"), 1)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(population))

#test for duplicates (same county but different data series)
county_pops |> count(region, year) |> filter(n > 1)



county_pops <- county_pops |>
    group_by(region, year) |>
    summarise(
        population = if (all(is.na(population))) NA_real_ else sum(population, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    )



county_pops |> count(region, year) |> filter(n > 1)

```

Let's combine the tables

```{r}
#A quick check before merging

county_pops |> count(region, year) |> filter(n > 1)
median_incomes |> count(region, year) |> filter(n > 1)


median_incomes <- inner_join(county_pops, median_incomes, 
                            by = join_by(region, year))
```

Maybe we don't need to change the data at all. It's necessary if we wish to make time
series for different counties, but not for maps. 

For this thesis it will suffice with a rough mapping of the counties to 
the different price zones. 

This is how we will map counties to price zones. 

This is based on definitions by snl. https://snl.no/prisomr%C3%A5der_for_str%C3%B8m

This is how i will map the counties to price zones, based on definitions by SNL.
Most of the counties that overlap price zones, do so in a negligable manner. 
Some exceptions are Telemark, buskerud and Vestland county. 
Since we are most interested in the effects of energy prices on people,
it makes sense to assign these overlapping counties to the price area
in which the majority of its population resides. 
Thus, i will make the simplification that vestland county resides in NO5,
Telemark resides in NO2, and buskerud in NO1. 


exception is vestland county, which is split almost perfectly in three between NO5, NO3 and NO2. 


NO1: Oslo, Akershus, Østfold, vestfold, Buskerud, Innlandet. 

NO2: Agder, Rogaland, Telemark, Vestfold

NO3: Møre og Romsdal, Trøndelag

NO4: Nordland, Troms, Finnmark

NO5: Southern parts of vestland.

price_zones <- c("NO1", "NO2", "NO3", "NO4", "NO5")
